interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between a MAC address and an IP address, and why do we need both?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate them cleanly by layer and scope. A MAC address is a **data-link-layer**, locally-scoped identifier, burned into the hardware by the manufacturer — it's meaningful only on the immediate physical link, and it gets **rewritten at every hop** as a frame crosses from one link to the next. An IP address is a **network-layer**, globally-routable identifier, assigned per network (statically or via DHCP) — it **stays the same end-to-end** across an entire multi-hop journey (barring NAT, which is its own layer of rewriting for a different reason).

We need both because they solve genuinely different problems, and conflating them is a common early-career confusion. IP answers "which network, and eventually which device, is this ultimately going to" — that's the job routing does, hop by hop, using IP prefixes that aggregate cleanly into manageable routing tables. MAC answers a much narrower question: "which specific device on *this* wire should receive this frame right now."

The mechanism that ties them together, worth walking through concretely: a router receiving a packet strips the incoming frame's MAC header entirely, looks only at the IP destination to make its routing decision (which interface should this go out?), then wraps the *same* IP packet in a **brand-new** Ethernet frame addressed to the next hop's MAC address — discovered via ARP for that specific next hop. The IP address is the constant thread through the whole journey; the MAC address is a fresh, local decision made independently at every hop.

**Testing:** whether you understand these as solving different problems at different layers with genuinely different lifetimes across a journey, not just "IP is bigger, MAC is smaller."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: MAC vs IP address

interviewQuestions.question: Why doesn't CSMA/CD matter on modern networks the way it used to?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point to a fundamental shift in the underlying medium, not an incremental protocol improvement. CSMA/CD exists specifically to manage collisions on a **shared** medium — one coax cable or a hub where every device's signal physically competes with every other device's on the same wire, and only one transmission can succeed at a time without garbling.

Modern switched Ethernet gives every device its own **dedicated, full-duplex** link straight to the switch — separate wire pairs for sending and receiving, with no other device's traffic sharing that physical segment at all. There's structurally nothing left to contend for and nothing to collide with, so CSMA/CD's entire reason for existing — detecting and recovering from a shared-medium collision — simply doesn't apply anymore.

CSMA/CD hardware is technically still part of the Ethernet standard, kept for backward compatibility with genuinely ancient shared-medium deployments, but on a full-duplex switched port it never activates — not "rarely triggers," but structurally cannot trigger, because a full-duplex link has no shared medium for two signals to collide on in the first place. I'd use this as an example of a mechanism that was essential given one network topology (shared bus/hub) and became vestigial the moment the underlying architecture changed (switched, full-duplex) — the protocol spec didn't need to remove it, the physical reality it was designed for just stopped occurring.

One place this still surfaces in interviews as a trick question: a **half-duplex** link (rare today, but possible with old hardware or misconfiguration) does still need CSMA/CD, since half-duplex by definition still shares the same wire for both directions. A duplex mismatch between two ends of a link is a real, if now uncommon, source of mysterious performance problems precisely because one side assumes full-duplex behavior and the other doesn't.

**Testing:** whether you understand CSMA/CD as solving a shared-medium problem specifically, not an inherent property of Ethernet as a protocol, and whether you know the half-duplex edge case that keeps it technically relevant.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why CSMA/CD faded away

interviewQuestions.question: A data-center team wants to enable jumbo frames to improve storage network throughput. What could go wrong, and how would you roll it out safely?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core risk is that jumbo frames only help if **every device on the path agrees** on the larger MTU — and the failure mode when they don't is unusually nasty because it doesn't look like a clean error.

If one switch, NIC, or virtual interface along the path is still configured for the standard 1500-byte MTU while everything else is set to 9000, packets larger than 1500 bytes hitting that device don't get a helpful rejection — they typically just get **silently dropped**, since fragmentation doesn't happen at layer 2 the way it can at layer 3. From the application's point of view, this shows up as a bizarre, hard-to-diagnose symptom: small requests work perfectly fine, but anything transferring a large payload mysteriously stalls, times out, or hangs — exactly the kind of intermittent, size-dependent failure that's expensive to root-cause because most people don't think to check MTU consistency first, since "it works sometimes" doesn't intuitively point at frame size.

My rollout plan: first, inventory every hop in the path — physical switches, NIC settings on every server, any virtual switches or bridges in a hypervisor layer, and any tunnel/overlay interfaces (VXLAN, etc.) that add their own encapsulation overhead and effectively need an even larger *underlying* MTU to carry a 9000-byte frame without fragmenting themselves. Second, change MTU on all of them **together**, not incrementally one hop at a time, since a mixed-MTU path during a staged rollout is exactly the silent-drop scenario I'm trying to avoid — there's no safe intermediate state here. Third, verify with `ping -s <size> -M do` (or equivalent) using packets sized right at the new MTU with the "don't fragment" flag set, from every meaningful pair of endpoints — this fails loudly and immediately if any hop disagrees, rather than waiting to discover it under production storage traffic. Only after that verification would I let real traffic use the new MTU.

**Testing:** whether you can anticipate the specific silent-failure mode of MTU mismatches (not just recite 'jumbo frames need consistent config') and design a verification step that catches it before production traffic does.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Rolling out jumbo frames safely
